top.line: What never scaled is on-demand expertise; agents can now carry the before and the after.
top.para: The book says old jobs that never scaled now can, and the editor asked for examples. The core is on-demand expertise. Each engagement has three phases: gathering context, a short meeting, and the write-up. The first and last took weeks and most experts dislike them. Agents can carry them, as the clinic does, so experts can work anywhere, even part-time.

in-short.line: Seven lines: on-demand expertise, three phases, the cost, the intersection, the clinic, agents, the opportunity.
in-short.para: What never scaled is getting someone's skills for the days you need them. The before and the after were the cost, so it happened only when company, talent, travel and budget lined up. The clinic works the other way. Agents can now be the support for any expert, which is an opportunity for experts and for service startups.

book.line: The book's section on jobs that never scaled, and the editor's request for three examples.
book.para: In Generation ZX Developers, the chapter Where do you land? ends with The jobs that never scaled, from You are lucky to be here. The editor's note asks for three examples of jobs that never scaled and now can, because without them the section is a claim without a case. This article is the case.

core.line: A consultant is someone with skills the team does not have: on-demand expertise is what never scaled.
core.para: Take a consultant: someone you bring in for skills the team lacks, for a while, not for ever. The core is getting the value of someone's skills for the days you need them. That never scaled, not because the skills were rare, but because of everything around them.

phases.line: Before, the meeting, after: about three weeks for a decent engagement.
phases.para: Before: the expert's questions are their experience; in application security the first is the CI pipeline, then team set-up, funding, rewards, non-functional requirements and scope. The meeting is short and prepared, connecting the pieces. After: writing it up for every audience. Traditionally a week or more, a day or two, and three days or more.

parts.line: Most experts dislike the first phase and hate the third, and are not hired for either.
parts.para: You bring an expert in for being a good architect, librarian, strategist or doctor, not a good writer. And the expert often understands the problem far better than the client, but can only write down what the client can take in, so much of it is lost.

agents.line: Agents can collect, filter and sanitise before, and write up for each audience after.
agents.para: Questionnaires and agents gather the context ahead of time, packaged and sanitised, so the expert arrives with a diagnosis to test. Afterwards agents turn decisions into actions, a roadmap and a version for each audience, so more of what the expert understood reaches the people who need it.

clinic.line: The clinic already works this way: others take the history, the specialist decides fast.
clinic.para: At a clinic, forms, reception and nurses collect your history; the specialist reads the key facts and decides; a team carries out the plan. The specialist is effective because everything around them protects their time. Agents can now be that support for any expert, without a building full of people.

intersection.line: Outside expertise needed a company, the right talent, someone who could travel, and a budget.
intersection.para: Consulting happened at an inefficient, expensive intersection, so it was used for specific things, mostly by big companies. The talent rarely lives near the client. When the context travels to the expert and the delivery travels back, the intersection stops mattering.

examples.line: Twelve jobs that never scaled, from historian and librarian to lawyer, doctor and translator.
examples.para: The historian gives a project its own history at the moments it matters; the librarian keeps everything findable; then the cartographer, architect, on-demand consultant, lawyer reviewing a contract, accountant, doctor, project manager, security lead, sherpa and translator. Agents can do parts, but they go in all directions; the expert gives the direction.

team.line: My SG/Send agent team has nineteen roles, many of which a project that size could never afford.
team.para: The historian tracks every decision and why; the librarian keeps knowledge connected; the cartographer maps the system; the accountant makes the money visible; with a sherpa, journalist and translator beside developers and architects. Each is a job that never scaled, now working for one project and directed by a person.

geeks.line: Every field has its geeks, with their own words and ontologies, and their limits make them good.
geeks.para: As a CISO I work with almost everyone, and most roles with agency attract a particular kind of person, with their own acronyms, definitions and passions. Their culture, experience and limitations shape their focus and make them good, and their value was locked behind the before and the after.

part-time.line: Twelve good hours: a part-time expert's time can now go on judgement, not gathering.
part-time.para: A parent working from home, or an expert who moved away from work they miss, may want twelve hours a week. Without support those hours went on gathering and writing, so part-time never paid. Companies spend little on making people productive; agents can be the department that does.

startups.line: Not Paul Graham's do things that don't scale: service businesses that never scaled now can.
startups.para: Graham's 2013 advice is to do unscalable things on purpose at the start. This is about companies bound by experts' hours: consultancies, agencies, specialist practices. Foundation Capital calls the shift Service-as-Software and estimates $4.6 trillion. With agents carrying the before and the after, a service grows with judgement, not hours.

for-the-book.line: Three examples for the chapter: the security consultant, the historian, and the librarian.
for-the-book.para: The on-demand security consultant: three weeks for two days of value, now two prepared days. The historian: every project needs one at a few moments, and now can have one. The librarian: making everything findable was always valuable and never staffed, and my agent does it daily.

related.line: The same shape elsewhere: graphs, removing code, minimum code, due diligence, reading.
related.para: Other articles describe things that never scaled and now can: graphs for everyone else, removing unused code, the minimum code below, due diligence as a form, and capturing what I learn from books; and the expert founders, best placed to build what comes next.

limits.line: Never scaled means for most companies; the timings are experience; the hours illustrative.
limits.para: Big firms did buy this work; most could not. The three weeks come from my experience, not a survey, and the twelve hours are illustrative. Agents carry the before and the after but do not replace the expert. The $4.6 trillion is an investor's estimate.

sources.line: A voice memo, the book's chapter and source article, the agent roles, Graham and Foundation Capital.
sources.para: A voice memo of 21 October 2026 prompted by the editor's note in the book; You are lucky to be here; the SG/Send agent team's role definitions; Paul Graham's Do Things that Don't Scale; and Foundation Capital on service as software, with related newsroom articles.
